issues.legal_issue: An unforeseen legal impediment that makes performance of a development contract impracticable can frustrate the contract despite terms requiring the developer to obtain approvals and accepting the land on an “as is where is” basis.
material_facts: A development authority auctioned land for a residential project, and the developer paid the full bid amount and entered into a development agreement.
The agreement made the developer responsible for obtaining approvals and clearances, and the auction terms offered the land on an “as is where is” basis.

Government agencies disputed whether the land was part of, or morphologically similar to, a protected ridge. They halted construction and required clearances from the Ridge Management Board and the Supreme Court before non-forestry use could proceed.

Environmental clearance was conditional on obtaining consent to establish from the pollution control committee. The committee required a ridge demarcation report, which the development authority did not provide, and consent was refused in the absence of the necessary clearances.
The developer took steps to begin the project and applied for the required consent, but the uncertainty and governmental impasse prevented construction.

The Supreme Court-appointed committee concluded that the land was outside the notified ridge but within the extended ridge, where the project required additional clearances and the Supreme Court’s permission.
The development authority had not contemplated that construction would be prohibited unless those additional clearances and permission were obtained.
issues.conclusion: The contract was frustrated under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act because the intervening circumstances made performance impracticable and were not contemplated by the parties. The development authority’s appeal was dismissed, and the developer was entitled to a refund of its deposit with the interest awarded by the High Court.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, “impossible” includes performance that becomes impracticable or useless in light of the contract’s purpose because an unforeseen supervening circumstance upsets the foundation of the bargain. If the parties contemplated the circumstance and agreed that performance would continue despite it, frustration does not apply. Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. explains this principle, drawing on Tamplin Steam Ship Co. Ltd. v. Anglo-Mexican Petroleum Products Co. Ltd. and Matthey v. Curling. The court distinguished Punjab Urban Planning & Development Authority v. Raghu Nath Gupta: an “as is where is” term concerns the physical condition and ordinary associated matters of the site, not construction prohibited by law absent additional permissions. The developer’s general approval obligations did not transfer the unanticipated impediment to it; the development authority had to ensure that the initial path to lawful construction was clear.

rule.if: contract_frustration_appeal and construction_blocked_by_unanticipated_legal_restriction and restriction_made_project_impracticable and parties_did_not_contemplate_restriction

predicates.contract_frustration_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning whether a development contract was frustrated.
predicates.construction_blocked_by_unanticipated_le: Government authorities prevented construction unless additional legal clearances or permissions were obtained.
predicates.restriction_made_project_impracticable: The restriction prevented the developer from carrying out the project despite its steps to obtain the approvals required for construction.
predicates.parties_did_not_contemplate_restriction: The parties did not contemplate that construction would be prohibited unless the additional clearances or permissions were obtained.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns frustration of a development contract, the rule treats the contract as frustrated and the deposit as returnable if an unanticipated legal restriction blocks construction, makes the project impracticable, and was not contemplated by the parties.

issues.legal_issue: An objection to the maintainability of a contractual writ petition is not considered when it is raised for the first time at the final hearing of an appeal after being omitted from the earlier proceedings.
material_facts: The development authority argued at the final hearing of its appeal that the writ petition was not maintainable because the dispute arose from a contract.
The development authority had not raised that objection before the High Court or in its petition to the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the maintainability objection because it was raised too late.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the procedural principle that an objection not raised before the lower court or in the petition initiating the appeal cannot be introduced for the first time at the final hearing. The Court did not decide the general maintainability of contractual writ petitions under Article 226.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: The proceeding is an appeal in which a party asks the appellate court to consider an objection.
predicates.maintainability_objection_first_raised_a: A party first argues at the final hearing that the underlying petition is not maintainable.
predicates.objection_omitted_from_earlier_proceedin: The party did not raise the objection before the lower court or in its appeal petition.

issues.definition: In an appeal, a maintainability objection first raised at the final hearing is not considered when the party omitted it from the earlier proceedings.

issues.legal_issue: A request to increase an interest award is declined when the recipient did not appeal that award, while the awarded interest is calculated from the date the full deposit was paid.
material_facts: The High Court awarded interest on the refundable deposit at a rate lower than the rate the developer had requested.
The developer did not appeal the High Court’s interest determination but asked the Supreme Court to increase the rate.
The entire deposit had been paid to the development authority on a single date.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to increase the interest rate and directed that interest be calculated from the date the full deposit was paid.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to alter the interest award because the developer had not appealed the High Court’s decision on interest. It clarified that interest on the deposit ran from the date the entire amount was paid. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this determination.

predicates.interest_award_appeal: The proceeding includes an appellate consideration of interest on a refundable deposit.
predicates.recipient_did_not_appeal_interest_determ: The recipient of the deposit did not appeal the lower court’s interest determination but sought a higher rate in the appellate court.
predicates.full_deposit_paid_before_refund: The payer had paid the full deposit before seeking its return.

issues.definition: When interest on a refundable deposit is considered on appeal, the existing rate remains in place if the recipient did not appeal the lower court’s interest determination, and interest runs from full payment of the deposit.
